screens.title: Synchronization and Critical Sections
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we examine why concurrent code can misbehave and how Java gives you tools to make it correct. You will learn what a race condition is and why seemingly simple operations like incrementing a counter fail under concurrency. Then we explore synchronization: the idea of a critical section and the monitor, also called an intrinsic lock. I will show how the synchronized keyword protects methods and blocks, and why sometimes you prefer a private lock object instead of synchronizing on this. You will also see the difference between object-level locks and class-level locks used by static synchronized methods. After covering locks we dive into coordinating threads with wait, notify and notifyAll and explain the important pattern: always wait inside a while loop to handle spurious wakeups. Finally, we preview common pitfalls including deadlock, livelock, and starvation and practical ways to avoid them, like consistent lock ordering and short critical sections. By the end, you will know the core primitives and when to apply them to keep shared state correct.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Synchronization
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Synchronization and Critical Sections

Understand race conditions, Java monitors, synchronized methods and blocks, wait/notify coordination, and practical pitfalls to avoid.

Race Condition
When thread interleavings make results unpredictable; example: two threads incrementing a shared counter.
Synchronization
Using locks so only one thread is inside a critical section at a time.
Coordination
wait, notify, notifyAll let threads signal state changes while releasing the lock.
Coming up
Code examples that fix races, producer-consumer coordination, and common pitfalls such as deadlocks.
Why it matters
Correct concurrent code avoids subtle data corruption in servers, tools, and background tasks.
Visual concept
Imagine a single whiteboard that multiple people try to update. Without a rule to take turns, messages overwrite each other. Synchronization gives a simple 'take the marker' rule so updates happen one at a time and the whiteboard remains consistent.
Explore Key Topics
Locks and monitors
Every object has a monitor; synchronized acquires it before running a critical section.
wait/notify pattern
Use wait inside a while loop and notify or notifyAll to resume waiting threads safely.
Pitfalls to avoid
Deadlocks arise from inconsistent lock ordering; design short critical sections and private locks.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part A
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will practice and verify. First, you will explain race conditions: what they are, how they arise from interleaved operations, and why they break correctness. For example, you will describe why two threads incrementing the same counter can leave one increment lost. Second, you will understand why shared mutable data needs synchronization: without it, simple read-modify-write sequences are not atomic and lead to inconsistent state. Each objective connects a definition with a concrete outcome so you know when to apply the idea. The third objective is about applying the synchronized keyword: you will be able to add synchronized to methods and narrow blocks to protect critical sections, and you will see code that uses a private lock object rather than synchronizing on this. Finally, you will start to differentiate object-level locks from class-level locks and recognize when a static synchronized method protects a class-wide resource. These skills let you both reason about concurrency bugs and fix them methodically.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part B
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives panel focuses on coordination and safe design. You will learn to use wait, notify and notifyAll to coordinate threads that produce and consume shared data, and why these calls must happen inside a synchronized context so the monitor semantics remain correct. You will practice the crucial pattern of using while loops around wait to handle spurious wakeups rather than relying on a single if check. Next, you will recognize common synchronization pitfalls: deadlock, where threads wait forever for each other's locks; livelock, where threads keep changing state without progress; and starvation, where one thread never gets the lock. Finally, you will acquire practical mitigation techniques: prefer short critical sections, use private final lock objects, acquire locks in a consistent order, and consider timeouts. Each objective pairs a clear rule with a concrete example so you can both identify and fix concurrency bugs in real Java code.

screens.title: Race Conditions: definition and classic counter example
screens.narratorSegment: A race condition occurs when the correctness of a program depends on the timing or ordering of thread operations. The classic example is a shared counter where two threads each perform a read, an increment, and a write. If both read before either writes, one increment is lost. This illustrates that operations you assume are atomic—like increment—are typically composed of multiple machine-level or JVM steps. Why this matters is practical: servers, background workers, and GUIs often share mutable objects. A lost update can corrupt application state, produce wrong totals, or break invariants. A common misconception is to assume that simply using a single field makes an operation safe; it does not. The remedy is to protect the critical section that spans read-modify-write using synchronization so that only one thread executes it at a time. Concrete example: if a counter starts at zero and two threads each run increment once, the unsynchronized outcome can be 1 instead of 2. Key takeaway: identify the read-modify-write sequences in your code and treat them as critical sections. A quick self-check: whenever an operation depends on a prior read of shared data, ask whether another thread could change that data before you finish.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Race Conditions
Core Concept

Race Conditions

A race condition is a correctness bug that arises from uncoordinated access to shared mutable data when multiple threads interleave their steps.

Concrete example
Two threads increment a shared counter: both read 0, both write 1. Expected 2, actual 1. The increment is not atomic.
Misconception
Fields by themselves are not thread-safe. Declaring a variable does not protect compound operations like increment.
Key Takeaway
Treat read-modify-write as a critical section and protect it with synchronization.
Step-by-step interleaving
  1. Thread A reads counter = 0
  2. Thread B reads counter = 0
  3. Thread A increments to 1 and writes 1
  4. Thread B increments its copy to 1 and writes 1 (overwrites A)
Try this thought check
Find each place in your code that does read-modify-write on shared state. If two threads could call it concurrently, it must be protected.

screens.title: Monitors and critical sections
screens.narratorSegment: Java associates every object with a monitor, often called an intrinsic lock or mutex. A monitor serializes access: when a thread acquires the lock, it becomes the only thread allowed to enter code synchronized on that monitor. The protected block is the critical section. This gives you a simple rule: before executing code that reads and writes shared mutable state, acquire the appropriate monitor. The basic lifecycle is: attempt to acquire the monitor; if successful, execute the critical section; finally, release the monitor so others can proceed. If the monitor is held, the thread blocks until it can obtain the lock. A mistake learners often make is to hold locks for too long or to synchronize code that doesn't need protection; this increases contention and reduces throughput. A practical guideline is to minimize the size of critical sections, keep locks private to avoid unintentional external contention, and document lock ownership. Example: protecting a bank account balance update requires locking around the update but not around time-consuming logging done afterward. Reflect: which objects in your design should own the monitor and why?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Monitors
Definition

Monitor (Intrinsic Lock)

An implicit lock associated with every Java object. Synchronized methods or blocks acquire the object's monitor to run a critical section exclusively.

Lifecycle
  • Attempt to acquire monitor
  • If held, block and wait
  • Execute critical section when acquired
  • Release monitor on exit
Design guidance
  • Prefer private final lock objects to avoid external contention.
  • Keep critical sections small; move slow work outside locks.
  • Document which code owns which locks and follow a consistent ordering.
Key Takeaway
Acquire the correct monitor for the data you protect and avoid holding locks longer than necessary.

screens.title: Synchronized instance methods (Counter example)
screens.narratorSegment: Here is a concrete code pattern that many Java developers use to prevent races: synchronized instance methods. When a method is declared synchronized, the thread must acquire the monitor of the instance, commonly called this, before executing the method body. This means two threads cannot both execute synchronized instance methods on the same object at the same time. The Counter example shows an integer field count and synchronized increment and getCount methods. In practice, synchronized methods are clear and simple, but they lock the entire method. If the method performs non-critical work such as logging or network input and output, you should prefer a synchronized block that covers only the necessary lines. A common misconception is that synchronizing one method protects all accesses to the field; only code synchronized on the same monitor participates in mutual exclusion. In other words, unsynchronized reads or writes bypass the lock. The takeaway: use synchronized instance methods for straightforward protection, and shrink critical sections when performance matters. Synchronized instance methods (Counter example) means a synchronized instance method acquires the monitor of the object (this) for mutual exclusion.. In practical terms, how synchronized methods lock on the instance monitor. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Synchronized Methods
Example

Counter with synchronized methods

Synchronized instance methods lock on the instance's monitor so only one thread can run them on the same object at a time.

<!-- Java code shown with HTML escapes -->
public class Counter {
  private int count = 0;

  // Synchronized instance method: locks on 'this' object
  public synchronized void increment() {
    count++;
    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " incremented to: " + count);
  }

  public synchronized int getCount() {
    return count;
  }
}
Notes and pitfalls
  • If other code updates count without the same lock, thread safety is broken.
  • Synchronized methods lock the whole method; use blocks to reduce contention.
Key Takeaway
Synchronized methods are a simple safety model but ensure all accesses to the protected field use the same monitor.

screens.title: Synchronized blocks and private lock objects
screens.narratorSegment: Synchronized blocks let you choose which object's monitor to acquire, and they allow you to limit the protected region to just the lines that need atomicity. A recommended pattern is to use a private final lock object instead of synchronizing on this or a public field. The private lock avoids accidental external synchronization by other code that might lock on the same object or a shared string literal. In the Balance example you create a final Object lock field and synchronize deposit and getAmount on that lock. This keeps the critical section minimal: read the current amount, compute the new value, and write back within the synchronized block. Non-critical work like artificial sleep or logging remains outside unless it also needs protection. A common misconception is that any object will do equally well; choosing a private lock isolates your synchronization policy. The takeaway: prefer private lock objects and narrow synchronized blocks to reduce contention and accidental coupling. Synchronized blocks and private lock objects means use a private final object as the lock to isolate synchronization and make critical sections explicit and small.. In practical terms, fine-grained control using an explicit lock object. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Synchronized Blocks
Pattern

Private lock object

Create a private final Object lock and synchronize on it to isolate your monitor and limit the protected region.

<!-- Java code with HTML escapes -->
public class Balance {
  private double amount = 0;
  private final Object lock = new Object(); // A dedicated lock object

  public void deposit(double value) {
    synchronized (lock) {
      double temp = amount; // Read current amount
      temp += value;        // Perform calculation
      try { Thread.sleep(10); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
      amount = temp;        // Write back
    }
  }

  public double getAmount() {
    synchronized (lock) { return amount; }
  }
}
Why prefer a private lock?
  • Prevents external code from acquiring your lock accidentally.
  • Allows you to synchronize on different locks for different data in the same object.
  • Reduces coupling and unexpected contention.
Common mistake
Synchronizing on this or on shared interned strings can create accidental global contention.

screens.title: Object-level vs Class-level locks
screens.narratorSegment: Java has two locking scopes to consider: object-level monitors and class-level monitors. Object-level locks are acquired when you synchronize on an instance or declare an instance method synchronized; they protect data associated with that particular object. Class-level locks are obtained when you synchronize on the Class object or declare a static synchronized method; they serialize access across all instances because the monitor is tied to the Class object itself. Use object-level locks when each instance has its own state to protect. Use class-level locks when you need to guard static state shared by all instances. A common misconception is assuming that synchronized instance methods and static synchronized methods interact: they do not share the same monitor. That means holding a class lock does not prevent another thread from entering an instance synchronized method on a particular object, unless that code also synchronizes on the Class object. Example: updating a static registry should be guarded by a class-level lock so concurrent calls across different instances do not corrupt the registry. Key design point: pick the lock whose scope matches the data's ownership.

keyIdea.text: Object locks protect instance data; class locks protect static, class-wide data. Choose the lock to match data ownership.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Lock Scope
Comparison

Object-level vs Class-level locks

Object-level lock
Acquired by synchronized instance methods or synchronized(instance). Protects data owned by that single instance.
  • Scope: per-instance
  • Use when each object has independent state
  • Lower contention across instances
Class-level lock
Acquired by static synchronized methods or synchronized(MyClass.class). Guards static shared state across all instances.
  • Scope: per-Class object
  • Use when protecting static registries or class-wide counters
  • Can cause broader contention
Design tip
Match the lock scope to the data ownership to avoid over-serialization and unexpected contention.

screens.title: wait(), notify(), notifyAll()
screens.narratorSegment: Java provides wait, notify, and notifyAll as a simple inter-thread communication mechanism built on monitors. A waiting thread calls object. wait() from inside a synchronized context: doing so releases the monitor and moves the thread into the WAITING state. Another thread, after changing the shared state, calls notify() or notifyAll() on the same object to wake waiting threads. notify() wakes one waiting thread nondeterministically; notifyAll() wakes all waiting threads which then contend to reacquire the lock. It is essential that wait and notify operate on the same monitor object, otherwise coordination fails. A frequent mistake is calling wait outside a synchronized block which triggers IllegalMonitorStateException; always call them while holding the lock. Also, never assume a single notify suffices; use a while loop when waiting to re-check the condition after waking. Example: a consumer waits while the queue is empty; when a producer adds an item it calls notifyAll() to wake consumers. Key takeaway: wait releases the lock atomically and lets other threads make progress before the waiting thread resumes. wait(), notify(), notifyAll() means wait releases the monitor and suspends a thread; notify/notifyall wake waiting threads to re-contend for the lock.. In practical terms, releasing the lock and coordinating thread activity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › wait / notify
Definition

wait(), notify(), notifyAll()

These methods coordinate threads on a shared monitor. wait releases the lock and suspends; notify or notifyAll wake waiting threads so they can re-acquire the lock and resume.

wait()
Releases the monitor and suspends the thread until notified. Must be called from synchronized code.
notify()
Wakes a single waiting thread. The selection is nondeterministic. Use when one waiter is sufficient.
notifyAll()
Wakes all waiting threads; they will contend for the monitor. Safer when multiple conditions may exist.
Practical rule
Always call wait()/notify()/notifyAll() from inside the same synchronized monitor and use while loops around wait to re-check conditions.

screens.title: Producer-Consumer with wait/notifyAll
screens.narratorSegment: The Producer-Consumer pattern shows coordination using wait and notifyAll. Producers add items to a bounded queue and consumers remove them. When the queue is full, a producer should wait until a consumer removes an item; when the queue is empty, a consumer waits until a producer adds one. Note the example uses a while loop around wait: while (queue. size() == capacity) { queue. wait(); } This is critical because of spurious wakeups: a thread can wake up without a notify call and must re-check the condition. After producing or consuming, call queue. notifyAll() to wake all waiters so they can re-check and proceed. A common misunderstanding is to use if instead of while around wait or to call notify without holding the same monitor. Also, prefer notifyAll when multiple types of waiters exist to avoid deadlocks. The concrete example uses synchronized(queue) blocks and the queue object as the shared monitor; that pattern is simple and effective for many use cases. Producer-Consumer with wait/notifyAll means use while loops around wait() and notifyall() to safely coordinate producers and consumers on a shared queue monitor.. In practical terms, a practical queue example and the while-wait pattern. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Producer-Consumer
Pattern

Producer-Consumer with wait/notifyAll

A bounded queue coordinates producers and consumers by waiting when full or empty and notifying when state changes.

<!-- Important parts of the MessageQueue -->
public void produce(String message) throws InterruptedException {
  synchronized (queue) {
    while (queue.size() == capacity) {
      queue.wait(); // release lock and wait
    }
    queue.add(message);
    queue.notifyAll(); // wake waiting consumers
  }
}

public String consume() throws InterruptedException {
  synchronized (queue) {
    while (queue.isEmpty()) {
      queue.wait(); // wait for producer
    }
    String message = queue.remove();
    queue.notifyAll(); // wake waiting producers
    return message;
  }
}
Why while, not if?
Spurious wakeups can resume a thread without a notify. Re-checking the condition prevents incorrect progress or exceptions.
Common mistake
Calling wait/notify outside synchronized blocks or using if around wait breaks the coordination contract.

screens.title: Deadlock, Livelock, and Starvation
screens.narratorSegment: Synchronization fixes races but introduces other hazards if misused. Deadlock happens when two or more threads wait forever for locks held by each other, for example Thread A holds Lock X and wants Lock Y while Thread B holds Lock Y and wants Lock X. Livelock is similar but threads keep reacting to each other and change state without making progress, while starvation means some thread is always denied access to a resource. To avoid deadlock, establish a consistent lock ordering and acquire locks in the same sequence across all threads. Prefer fine-grained locking and short critical sections so threads hold locks for less time. When absolute safety is needed, use timeouts or higher-level concurrency utilities not covered here. A common misconception is that adding more locks reduces contention; in fact, poorly ordered multiple locks increase deadlock risk. Reflect: audit any code that acquires multiple locks and enforce a global ordering or reduce lock usage. The practical insight is that careful design prevents these complex failure modes. Deadlock, Livelock, and Starvation means deadlock and related hazards arise when locks are acquired inconsistently or held too long; use ordering and minimal critical sections to reduce risk.. In practical terms, recognize and avoid common concurrency hazards. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Pitfalls
Pitfall

Deadlock, Livelock, Starvation

These are the main hazards introduced by synchronization when locks interact improperly or threads are unfairly scheduled.

Deadlock
Threads wait forever for resources held by each other. Common cause: inconsistent lock ordering.
Livelock
Threads repeatedly change state in response to each other but make no forward progress.
Starvation
A thread never acquires the lock due to scheduling or other threads always taking it first.
Mitigations
  • Enforce consistent lock ordering across the codebase.
  • Keep critical sections short and avoid nested locks when possible.
  • Consider timeouts or higher-level concurrency utilities for complex cases.

screens.title: Design rules for safe synchronization
screens.narratorSegment: When you design synchronized code, follow a compact set of rules that reduce errors and keep performance reasonable. First, identify the minimal critical section and move any non-essential work—like logging, input and output, or long computations—outside the synchronized block. Second, prefer private final lock objects so external code cannot interfere with your monitor. Third, keep lock acquisition order consistent across all components to prevent circular waits and deadlocks. Fourth, prefer notifyAll when multiple conditions may be present or if you are unsure which waiter to awaken, and always wait within a while loop so spurious wakeups are harmless. Fifth, validate that all reads and writes of the protected data use the same monitor; one unsynchronized access breaks the contract. Finally, measure: make sure contention is acceptable, and refactor to more granular locks when necessary. A common misconception is that more synchronization always improves safety; poorly designed locks can reduce throughput and introduce complex bugs. The takeaway: clear ownership, minimal scope, and consistent ordering are your best defenses. Design rules for safe synchronization means minimize critical sections, use private lock objects, be consistent with lock ordering, and validate that all accesses use the same monitor.. Best Practices

Design rules for safe synchronization

Minimal critical sections
Protect only what you must. Move slow operations outside synchronized blocks to reduce contention.
Private lock objects
Use private final Object locks to avoid accidental external synchronization and to separate concerns.
Consistent ordering
When acquiring multiple locks, always acquire them in a global consistent order to prevent deadlocks.
Wait/notify discipline
Always wait inside while loops and call notify/notifyAll while holding the same monitor.

Good synchronization is about clear ownership, minimal scope, and consistent rules—these reduce both bugs and contention.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we examine why concurrent code can misbehave and how Java gives you tools to make it correct. You will learn what a race condition is and why seemingly simple operations like incrementing a counter fail under concurrency. Then we explore synchronization: the idea of a critical section and the monitor, also called an intrinsic lock. I will show how the synchronized keyword protects methods and blocks, and why sometimes you prefer a private lock object instead of synchronizing on this. You will also see the difference between object-level locks and class-level locks used by static synchronized methods. After covering locks we dive into coordinating threads with wait, notify and notifyAll and explain the important pattern: always wait inside a while loop to handle spurious wakeups. Finally, we preview common pitfalls including deadlock, livelock, and starvation and practical ways to avoid them, like consistent lock ordering and short critical sections. By the end, you will know the core primitives and when to apply them to keep shared state correct.

These objectives map to practical skills you will practice and verify. First, you will explain race conditions: what they are, how they arise from interleaved operations, and why they break correctness. For example, you will describe why two threads incrementing the same counter can leave one increment lost. Second, you will understand why shared mutable data needs synchronization: without it, simple read-modify-write sequences are not atomic and lead to inconsistent state. Each objective connects a definition with a concrete outcome so you know when to apply the idea. The third objective is about applying the synchronized keyword: you will be able to add synchronized to methods and narrow blocks to protect critical sections, and you will see code that uses a private lock object rather than synchronizing on this. Finally, you will start to differentiate object-level locks from class-level locks and recognize when a static synchronized method protects a class-wide resource. These skills let you both reason about concurrency bugs and fix them methodically.

This second objectives panel focuses on coordination and safe design. You will learn to use wait, notify and notifyAll to coordinate threads that produce and consume shared data, and why these calls must happen inside a synchronized context so the monitor semantics remain correct. You will practice the crucial pattern of using while loops around wait to handle spurious wakeups rather than relying on a single if check. Next, you will recognize common synchronization pitfalls: deadlock, where threads wait forever for each other's locks; livelock, where threads keep changing state without progress; and starvation, where one thread never gets the lock. Finally, you will acquire practical mitigation techniques: prefer short critical sections, use private final lock objects, acquire locks in a consistent order, and consider timeouts. Each objective pairs a clear rule with a concrete example so you can both identify and fix concurrency bugs in real Java code.

A race condition occurs when the correctness of a program depends on the timing or ordering of thread operations. The classic example is a shared counter where two threads each perform a read, an increment, and a write. If both read before either writes, one increment is lost. This illustrates that operations you assume are atomic—like increment—are typically composed of multiple machine-level or JVM steps. Why this matters is practical: servers, background workers, and GUIs often share mutable objects. A lost update can corrupt application state, produce wrong totals, or break invariants. A common misconception is to assume that simply using a single field makes an operation safe; it does not. The remedy is to protect the critical section that spans read-modify-write using synchronization so that only one thread executes it at a time. Concrete example: if a counter starts at zero and two threads each run increment once, the unsynchronized outcome can be 1 instead of 2. Key takeaway: identify the read-modify-write sequences in your code and treat them as critical sections. A quick self-check: whenever an operation depends on a prior read of shared data, ask whether another thread could change that data before you finish.

Java associates every object with a monitor, often called an intrinsic lock or mutex. A monitor serializes access: when a thread acquires the lock, it becomes the only thread allowed to enter code synchronized on that monitor. The protected block is the critical section. This gives you a simple rule: before executing code that reads and writes shared mutable state, acquire the appropriate monitor. The basic lifecycle is: attempt to acquire the monitor; if successful, execute the critical section; finally, release the monitor so others can proceed. If the monitor is held, the thread blocks until it can obtain the lock. A mistake learners often make is to hold locks for too long or to synchronize code that doesn't need protection; this increases contention and reduces throughput. A practical guideline is to minimize the size of critical sections, keep locks private to avoid unintentional external contention, and document lock ownership. Example: protecting a bank account balance update requires locking around the update but not around time-consuming logging done afterward. Reflect: which objects in your design should own the monitor and why?

Here is a concrete code pattern that many Java developers use to prevent races: synchronized instance methods. When a method is declared synchronized, the thread must acquire the monitor of the instance, commonly called this, before executing the method body. This means two threads cannot both execute synchronized instance methods on the same object at the same time. The Counter example shows an integer field count and synchronized increment and getCount methods. In practice, synchronized methods are clear and simple, but they lock the entire method. If the method performs non-critical work such as logging or network input and output, you should prefer a synchronized block that covers only the necessary lines. A common misconception is that synchronizing one method protects all accesses to the field; only code synchronized on the same monitor participates in mutual exclusion. In other words, unsynchronized reads or writes bypass the lock. The takeaway: use synchronized instance methods for straightforward protection, and shrink critical sections when performance matters. Synchronized instance methods (Counter example) means a synchronized instance method acquires the monitor of the object (this) for mutual exclusion.. In practical terms, how synchronized methods lock on the instance monitor. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Synchronized blocks let you choose which object's monitor to acquire, and they allow you to limit the protected region to just the lines that need atomicity. A recommended pattern is to use a private final lock object instead of synchronizing on this or a public field. The private lock avoids accidental external synchronization by other code that might lock on the same object or a shared string literal. In the Balance example you create a final Object lock field and synchronize deposit and getAmount on that lock. This keeps the critical section minimal: read the current amount, compute the new value, and write back within the synchronized block. Non-critical work like artificial sleep or logging remains outside unless it also needs protection. A common misconception is that any object will do equally well; choosing a private lock isolates your synchronization policy. The takeaway: prefer private lock objects and narrow synchronized blocks to reduce contention and accidental coupling. Java has two locking scopes to consider: object-level monitors and class-level monitors. Object-level locks are acquired when you synchronize on an instance or declare an instance method synchronized; they protect data associated with that particular object. Class-level locks are obtained when you synchronize on the Class object or declare a static synchronized method; they serialize access across all instances because the monitor is tied to the Class object itself. Use object-level locks when each instance has its own state to protect. Use class-level locks when you need to guard static state shared by all instances. A common misconception is assuming that synchronized instance methods and static synchronized methods interact: they do not share the same monitor. That means holding a class lock does not prevent another thread from entering an instance synchronized method on a particular object, unless that code also synchronizes on the Class object. Example: updating a static registry should be guarded by a class-level lock so concurrent calls across different instances do not corrupt the registry. Key design point: pick the lock whose scope matches the data's ownership.

Java provides wait, notify, and notifyAll as a simple inter-thread communication mechanism built on monitors. A waiting thread calls object. wait() from inside a synchronized context: doing so releases the monitor and moves the thread into the WAITING state. Another thread, after changing the shared state, calls notify() or notifyAll() on the same object to wake waiting threads. notify() wakes one waiting thread nondeterministically; notifyAll() wakes all waiting threads which then contend to reacquire the lock. Also, never assume a single notify suffices; use a while loop when waiting to re-check the condition after waking. Review the fundamental terms from this chapter so they stick: a race condition is an outcome that depends on the timing of threads and can cause lost updates. Thread safety is the property of code that behaves correctly when accessed concurrently without additional synchronization. Synchronization is the practice of using locks or monitors so only one thread executes a critical section at a time. Critical section refers to the code that accesses shared mutable resources and must be protected. These compact definitions will help you identify which parts of your code need protection and which do not. Keep these practical primitives in mind: the monitor is the intrinsic lock every object has; synchronized protects critical sections by acquiring that monitor. Use synchronized methods for simple cases and synchronized blocks with private lock objects for fine-grained control. For coordination use wait to release the monitor and suspend, and notify or notifyAll to wake waiters, always inside a synchronized block. Remember the while-loop around wait to handle spurious wakeups. Finally, watch for deadlocks and other hazards: avoid nested locks without clear ordering and keep critical sections minimal.
